notes.edition_2: Prints the heading as σύνοψις ἠκριβωμένη, with H, Par. and V; Bas. alone has ἠκριβωμένη σύνοψις (ΗΚΡΙΒΩΜΕΝΗ ΣΥΝΟΨΙΣ), recorded in the apparatus as a difference of word order. Par., the reprint of the editio princeps, prints ΤΗΣ ΜΟΥΣΙΚΗΣ ΣΥΝΟ-|ψις ἠκριβωμένη. H writes the heading between crosses; V writes it in red. The 1556 order of Bas. is most likely a typographical rearrangement for the two-line heading in capitals. The sense is the same.

notes.edition_1: Prints εἰ γὰρ μὴ with H, Par. and V; Bas. alone has δὲ (γὰρ H Par. V] δὲ Bas.). The γάρ clause explains why a note that could not be fitted to another is not ἐναρμόνιος (24.20–23). Bas. apparently prints εἰ δ’ μὴ, with δ’ elided before a consonant and a clear elision mark; δ’ or δέ, the word is the same. Such an elision is anomalous and points to a misprint, possibly a misread γάρ compendium in the printer's copy (Par. prints γάρ here with a κ-like compendium sort), rather than a deliberate correction by Xylander. δέ would also be good Greek and good sense ('but if it is not so uttered…'): an adversative continuation instead of the explanatory 'for'. Translations made from Bas. read δέ.
notes.edition_2: No note: the edition prints this reading without comment.

notes.edition_1: Prints ὑπάτη διάτονος as transmitted, without obeli. Bas., Par., H and V all have ὑπάτη, and H writes it in full. The standard name of this 4th note is λιχανὸς ὑπάτων διάτονος (Cleonides, Isag. 4) or διάτονος ὑπάτων (Gaudentius, Harm. intr. 6), the qualifier being regularly the genitive plural of the tetrachord. But the author's names are non-standard elsewhere too (adjectival τρίτη / διάτονος / νήτη διεζευγμένη for διεζευγμένων; παράμεσος for παραμέση), so 'the diatonic hypate' is kept as his naming, although διάτονος ὑπερβολαίων (25.10) shows that he knew the genitive-plural pattern. Possible conjectures: ὑπάτων διάτονος (an early misreading of a suspended -ων among the surrounding ὑπάτη), or διάτονος ὑπάτων (his order for the other tetrachords, and Gaudentius' form, but needing a transposition).
notes.edition_2: Prints †ὑπάτη διάτονος† between obeli. The transmitted note name is problematic in the Greater Perfect System: the expected name is ὑπάτων διάτονος (lichanos hypaton). But all four witnesses (Bas. 25.6; H 64v.19; Par. 21v.8; V 76r.21) have the same substantive wording, and no witness supports the correction, so the words are kept, between obeli. The note names before and after it establish the position of this note in the system.

notes.edition_1: Prints μέση μόνως with Bas., Par. and V. At the line end (64v.20) H has μόν with a curl over ν, a suspension whose expansion is doubtful: μόν(ος), μόν(η) and μόν(ον) are possible, and a compendium for μόν(ως) cannot be excluded, so the sign does not decide the ending. The adverb gives 'just mese', the name with no tetrachord qualifier after a run of names in …μέσων. The adjective μόνος / μόνη would mean 'mese alone, single', possibly that the mese is counted once, as the end of the first octachord and the start of the second (25.12-14). H is recorded because an adjective with μέση differs from the adverb: μόνως Bas. Par. V] μόν(ος) H (suspension, expansion doubtful).
notes.edition_2: Prints μέση †μόνος† between obeli. μέση μόνος is doubtful both grammatically and as a technical term. H (64v.20) has an abbreviation, μόν(ος), whose expansion is uncertain; V (76v.2) has μόνως, which may be the original reading. The H abbreviation and the V variant are kept distinct, and the word is obelized rather than given a conjectural meaning without notice.

notes.edition_1: Prints ὅσον ὀκτὼ ἥμισυ … ὅσον ὀκτὼ τέταρτον. ὅσον is in H, the oldest witness, and V; Bas. and Par. have οἷον, agreeing also in an error at 25.22 (ἔχον) and in ὀκτωτέταρτον (25.25), probably from the Venice princeps of 1532, which Par. reprints. The clauses are parallel, the second ὅσον is in all witnesses, and ὅσον expresses the quantity. οἷον ('as it were 8½') also makes sense, as illustration, and the variatio is less expected (levelling is easy), but it softens a figure justified at 26.1-2. Xylander's marginal τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς («addo», twice; 'half / a quarter of the ratio 9 : 8') is unnecessary: the transmitted 8½ and 8¼ lie between 8 and 9, and 26.1-2 (the unit undivided in numbers, divided in matter) justifies this halving.
notes.edition_2: Prints Xylander's marginal supplement ⟨τοῦ ἐννέα πρὸς⟩ before ὀκτὼ in both clauses, as a conjecture. At 25.24 Bas. has an asterisk before ὀκτὼ; the supplement makes explicit the numerator and the relation of the ratio. The words are absent from H, Par. and V; H has related ratio diagrams, but not these words. At 25.25 Bas. has † before ὀκτὼ, and the supplement is repeated there as Xylander's margin directs; no witness has the words. οἷον in the first clause is printed without comment.

notes.edition_1: Prints ἑξκαιδέκατον (and ἑξκαιδέκατος at 29.20), and the same form as a conjecture in P fr. 1 (Vinc. 338.17: ἑξκαιδέκατον coni.] ἑνδέκατον P | ἑξδέκατον Vinc.). The number must be 16: it is called a square (4²), and its half (τὰ ὀκτώ) and its double (τριακονταδύο) are not squares, as the text says. P's 11 (Vincent: 'Ms. ἑνδ.', the full form inferred) is not a square, so impossible. ἑξκαιδέκατος is an LSJ lemma of its own (Hp. Epid. 1.26), beside ἑκκαιδέκατος (Hdt. 2.143, etc.), whose entry does not mention it. Vincent's ἑξδέκατον changes the fewest letters but has no LSJ entry. Alternatives: classical ἑκκαιδέκατον, or a cardinal ἑκκαίδεκα (perhaps a numeral ιϛʹ misread as ιαʹ; cf. τὰ ὀκτώ, τὸν τριακονταδύο ἀριθμόν). Only the spelling is uncertain.

notes.edition_1: Prints σύμφρασις (338.4) and τὴν σύμφρασιν (338.7), the word as reported from P. The context requires combination or fusion of magnitudes, and συμφθάρσεως in the main text (Bas. 27.10, 32.10–11, 32.17) shows that fusion terminology is used here. The reported σύμφρασις may be a corruption or a terminological formation, but no single restoration is claimed. Vincent's note (338 n. 1) proposes σύγχρασις, not σύγκρασις. At 338.7 Vincent's accusative replaces P's nominative ἡ σύμφρασις; the construction ἐγγίνεται … εἶναι remains awkward, but the report does not justify further silent alteration.
notes.edition_2: Prints the conjecture σύμφθαρσις at 338.4 and 338.7 (σύμφρασις P | σύγκρασις Vinc. in nota). The passage justifies the claim that an incomposite interval sounds as one ἐκ συμφθάρσεως (27.10, all witnesses) and fits only fusion: immaterial, unmoving numbers do not fuse; melody, continuous in matter, combines the length over two strings into one. LSJ s.v. σύμφθαρσις 2: 'melting into one another' (Hermog. Id. 1.12; cf. Iamb. in Nic. p. 80 P.); s.v. σύμφρασις only 'continuous speech' (Hdn.Gr., Phot.). The corruption (loss of θ, αρ/ρα metathesis, a rare word made familiar) is easy; P garbles the word in fr. 2 too (ἐξυφθάρσεως, Vinc. 340 n. 2). Against: P has σύμφρασις consistently, twice, needing a forced sense ('joining together into continuity'). Fr. 2's mixing vocabulary (κίρνανται) gives σύγκρασις some appeal.

notes.edition_1: Prints τελειούμενον with H, Par. and V, recording τελούμενον Bas. Bas. stands alone against H, the oldest witness, and against Par. and V. Its τελούμενον is an easy assimilation to τελούμενον in the line above (27.25, the fifth, unanimous); the reverse change would have had to happen independently in H, in Par.'s source and in V. τελειόω, 'to bring to completion, to perfect', suits the octave as the complete system (ἐν τῷ ὀκταχόρδῳ τῶν ὅλων διαστάσεων συμπληρουμένων, 28.2–4). The difference in sense is slight: τελειούμενον may suggest the octave as the 'perfect' or complete system, whereas the fifth is only τελούμενον.

notes.edition_2: Prints ἐπαναδιπλουμένων with H, Par. and V, recording ἀναδιπλουμένων Bas. Bas. stands alone against the three witnesses. ἐπαναδιπλόω, 'to repeat yet again; pass. to be repeated', is a well-attested compound (LSJ cites Arist. Pr. 910b25 and Gal. 15.879; pass. Arist. APr. 49a11, Metaph. 1003b28) and goes naturally with αὖθις. The loss of ἐπ- in Bas. is a simple shortening, either a misprint or Xylander's simplification. In H and Par. the word is divided across lines (ἐπανα|διπλουμένων H 66v.11–12; ἐπα|ναδιπλουμένων Par. 23v.10–11).

notes.edition_1: Prints Xylander's marginal corrections as conjectures: {δὶς} ⟨διὰ πασῶν καὶ⟩ διὰ τεσσάρων and {δὶς} ⟨διὰ πασῶν καὶ⟩ διὰ πέντε. The compound intervals, octave plus fourth and octave plus fifth, are meant, although Bas., H, Par. and V all have δὶς; braces mark the deletion and angle brackets the addition. In Bas. the asterisk of the first marginal note stands before δὶς διὰ τεσσάρων. The dagger keying the second is printed before the final δὶς διὰ πασῶν, but its margin names the octave plus fifth, so the correction is applied to the preceding δὶς διὰ πέντε and the double octave is kept; this placement is a judgment. The ratios and the following terminology support the intended correction.
notes.edition_2: Prints δὶς διὰ τεσσάρων … δὶς διὰ πέντε, recording Xylander's marginal διὰ πασῶν καὶ διὰ τεσσάρων / πέντε. The names are unanimous, recur at 28.6–7 without marginal note and appear in P fr. 2 (Vinc. 340.8–9): the author's usage. The sense is the fourth and fifth again over the octave (8:3, 3:1), redoubled from the octachord (κἀκεῖθεν αὖθις, 28.4) and classed κατὰ ἀντίφωνον; a literal double fourth (16:9) or fifth (9:4) is no consonance in any Greek theorist. Theon, Expos. pp. 48.17–20 (κατ' ἀντίφωνον only octave and double octave), 52.1–7 (octave plus fourth or fifth), 51.4–20 Hiller (names from the octachord lyre), explains Xylander's notes without deciding the reading. His † stands before δὶς διὰ πασῶν (28.12), but by sense belongs to δὶς διὰ πέντε, not to the double octave.

notes.edition_1: No note: the edition prints this reading without comment.
notes.edition_2: Prints βαρεῖ with Bas. and V, recording βάρει H Par. The difference is in the accent only, but βάρει is the dative of βάρος ('weight') and gives no sense against τοῦ ὀξέος; the two accentuations give two different words (the adjective βαρύς, the noun βάρος), and H and Par. agree on the noun. In H (βά|ρει, divided at the line end) it is probably a mere misplaced accent. Bas. prints βαρεί, with an acute, an accent misprint.

notes.edition_1: Prints {δὶς} at 29.8 and 29.9, following Xylander's marginal deletion, keyed in Bas. by asterisks. The deletion removes a redundant doubling after διὰ πασῶν; H, Par. and V keep δὶς. The same error stands in the octave-plus-fifth term at 29.9, and the following list of ratios confirms the mathematical identification.
notes.edition_2: Prints δὶς with Bas., H, Par. and V, recording Xylander's deletion; his margin, keyed by asterisks to δὶς here and at 29.9, reads «abundant omnino, et delenda sunt». Whichever is printed, the intervals meant are the octave plus a fourth, δι’ ὀκτὼ καὶ ἡμιτονίου (8½ tones = 6 + 2½; 8:3, exemplified 16:6), and the octave plus a fifth, δι’ ἐννέα καὶ ἡμιτονίου (9½ tones = 6 + 3½; 3:1, exemplified 18:6), not the octave and twice the fourth or fifth, which would be 11 and 13 tones (32:9 and 9:2). δὶς marks the fourth or fifth 'again', in the second octave, as in P's τὸ δὶς διὰ τεσσάρων, and is not a multiplier. Without δὶς the text gives the classical names.

notes.edition_1: No note: the edition prints this reading without comment.
notes.edition_2: Prints τοῦ διὰ πασῶν (H Par. V): Bas. alone has δὲ, apparently a regularisation, since the last two items are asyndetic and no witness has δὲ at 29.15. Prints δὶς at 29.14 (H V; Bas. Par. omit) and 29.15 (H Par. V; Bas. omits). δὶς stands throughout the tradition: H and V at all four places (29.8, 29.9, 29.14, 29.15), Par. at three, Bas. at 29.8-9 (with Xylander's «abundant omnino, et delenda sunt»), its omission at 29.14-15 presumably being his silent correction. P's addition has τὸ δὶς διὰ τεσσάρων, τὸ δὶς διὰ πέντε. It is the tradition's own non-classical name (classical: Eucl. Sect. can. 12, Ptol. Harm. 1.5-6), not to be classicised; the figures (8½ tones, 8:3 = 16:6; 9½ tones, 3:1 = 18:6) show octave plus fourth and fifth.

notes.edition_2: Prints the conjecture προσλαμβανόμενον (P προλαμβανόμενον). Vincent prints προ-|λαμβανόμενον, divided at his line end, without note; the loss of a single σ after πρὸς τὸν, in P or in his print, would be trivial. προσλαμβανόμενος, the technical name of the lowest note of the Greater Perfect System, is the author's own name for note 1 (25.4–5, all witnesses); προλαμβανόμενος ('taken first') is not a note name. The six ἔμμεσα listed are exactly the intervals from note 1: the base term 6 (29.17–23) stands for note 1, and 8, 9, 12, 16, 18, 24 for notes 4, 5, 8, 11, 12, 15 (cf. 28.19–22). P's form, 'the note taken first', i.e. the base term (cf. 29.17 κείσθω πρῶτος ἐν ἀριθμοῖς ὅρος), gives a tolerable sense; both refer to the same note.

notes.edition_1: Prints the conjecture ἐκ συμφθάρσεως twice (ἐξυφθάρσεως P | ἐξ φθάρσεως Vinc.). Vinc. 340 n. 2, the only report of the manuscript, gives 'Ms. ἐξυφθάρσεως', unknown to dictionaries. Vincent's division gives neither grammar (ἐξ before φ) nor sense. The conjecture keeps every letter of -υφθάρσεως, needing only phonetic ἐξ- for ἐκ σ- (κσ = ξ) and loss of μ before φ. Decisive: the author's own phrase, with the same ἓν … διάστημα (27.10; 32.10–11; 32.17), and fr. 1 argues about the same σύμφθαρσις, garbled there (σύμφρασις). LSJ s.v. σύμφθαρσις: joint destruction of a mixture's components (Alex. Aphr. Mixt. 216.24), 'melting into one another' (Hermog. Id. 1.12; cf. Iambl. in Nic. p. 80 Pistelli), the sense κίρνανται and εἰς ἓν διάστημα require. ἐκ συνθέσεως and ἐξ ὑφάνσεως are not palaeographically compelling.
notes.edition_2: Prints Vincent's ἐξ φθάρσεως at both places. The manuscript reading ἐξυφθάρσεως is an indirect, unexplained report (Vinc. 340 n. 2). It may conceal a compressed or corrupt ἐκ συμφθάρσεως: the exact internal parallel is Bas. 27.10 and 32.10–11, 17 (also H and V at those places), where the phrase denotes the fusion of intervals, so the word need not be treated as a wholly unrelated technical noun. This explains the context, but does not prove the spelling of the unseen manuscript.

notes.edition_1: Prints Vincent's κεκραμένων (Vinc. 340 n. 4; P κεκρυμμένων). κεκρυμμένων is an ordinary participle meaning 'concealed'; κεκραμένων fits the repeated argument about fusion and mixture and the following κίρνανται. Confusion between the two formations is plausible, though the report alone cannot settle whether P intentionally used κεκρυμμένων.
notes.edition_2: Prints P's κεκρυμμένων (Vinc. 340 n. 4: 'Ms. κεκρυμμένων'), recording κεκραμένων Vinc. P's reading, 'the intervals contained (latent) in them', gives good sense, so it is kept. Vincent's κεκραμένων, 'the intervals mixed in them', echoes κίρνανται ('are blended') at the end of the sentence. Both give good sense.

notes.edition_1: Prints P's ὅτι μηδὲ τοῖς ἀριθμητικοῖς τοῦτο δέδοκται (Vinc. 342.4), recording Vincent's ὅ, τι … οὔ πω; Vincent's notes (nn. 2-3) give 'Ms. ὅτι', 'Ms. τοῦτο'. P's text is sound: 'since not even the arithmeticians have accepted this', that is, the division of the unit. Vincent's change creates a doubled negative (μηδὲ … οὔ πω). His printed text ('a thing that not even the arithmeticians have yet accepted') is the one readers of Vincent will know; the sense is nearly the same.
notes.edition_2: No note: the edition prints this reading without comment.

notes.edition_1: Prints γοερώτερον with H (69r.19, abbreviated γοερώτερο(ν)), recording γοέτερον Bas. Par. V. γοέτερον is not a Greek form: the comparative of γοερός (short syllable before the ending) is regularly γοερώτερος, like σοφώτερος. LSJ s.v. γοερός gives no comparative, so this is a regular formation, not a recorded rarity. The syllable -ρω- was lost, perhaps under the influence of the familiar ending -έτερος (ἡμέτερος, ἑκάτερος). Par. and V share the error, so it is not a misprint of Bas. but an error of the branch from which the printed text comes; the shared error links V to the printed tradition. The oldest witness keeps the correct form.
notes.edition_2: Prints γοέτερον with Bas., Par. and V; H (69r.19) has the fuller γοερώτερ(ον). The fuller form alone is not sufficient reason to classicise what may be the author's own usage.
